newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: China fights back against censure in UN rights body.
newsitem.headline: China fights back against censure in UN rights body.

text.p: China has launched a rearguard action at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva to head off a resolution condemning it for abusing human rights, diplomats said on Sunday.

They said China, which has fought off previous such resolutions by rallying enough support for "no action" motions annually since 1990, was actively lobbying other countries to block this year's Danish-sponsored resolution and that it might succeed again.
"The Chinese are working like hell to save their skin," said one diplomat.

Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said at the weekend his country had decided to table the resolution at the 53-member U.N. Human Rights Commission after European Union discord foiled attempts to draft a joint EU motion.

"Because of internal disagreement in the EU a situation arose where it looked as if no resolution on China would be proposed this year. I find this completely unacceptable," Sunday's edition of the Berlingske Tidende quoted him as saying.
The Netherlands, as holder of the rotating EU presidency, was expected to present the annual EU-sponsored resolution on China on behalf of its 15 members with strong backing from the United States.

But France declared last week that dialogue with China was better than confrontation, and Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, in a letter to his EU colleagues early this week, said he understood three member states, who diplomats said were Germany, Spain and Italy, had taken a similar position.
Without these key member states on board, Van Mierlo suggested the Netherlands would not table a joint EU motion.
The United States and Britain both welcomed Denmark's decision and offered to co-sponsor the resolution.
"This decision by Denmark reflects its principled commitment to the universality of human rights," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in a statement on Saturday.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind also said Britain would join the United States in co-sponsoring the resolution.
Diplomats said Denmark was expected to table the resolution early this week but its wording had yet to be finalised.

Bill Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, last week said he would be engaged in "quite active lobbying" against the "no action" motion and would aim at what he called "eight or nine swing votes that are moving rapidly".
Every year since Beijing's bloody crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in 1989, China has gathered enough support to block resolutions condemning its human rights record.
Last year, it rallied the support of Asian nations including Indonesia, Malaysia, Pakistan, India, Belarus, Cuba, Egypt, Uganda, Ethiopia and Algeria, diplomats said.
Russia, which abstained last year, and Ukraine, which backed the motion, have yet to make their positions clear, they said.
China has accused the West of using the body to attack developing countries which have an overall majority at the forum.
Rights groups say the highly politicised Commission is becoming irrelevant, with powerful countries working hard backstage to ensure allies do not come under full scrutiny.

"The Commission is unable to address the situation in China," said Isabelle Scherer, Geneva representative of the Amnesty International, which said on Friday that China executed 3,500 prisoners in 1996 and was making increasing use of the death penalty in its year-old "strike hard" anti-crime drive.
"The Commission is losing its credibility. It doesn't reflect the realities of the human rights world any more. There is a danger it may become a farce," she said.
